opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this came out of our work on FourCastNet and moving from the original Fourier neural operator to the spherical Fourier neural operator. The basic issue is that the original FNO uses the standard FFT, which implicitly assumes your domain is a flat, periodic rectangle, like a torus. The Earth isn't that. When you take a lat-lon grid and treat it as a flat rectangle, you get distortions near the poles, you break the symmetries of the sphere, and you introduce artifacts at the boundaries. For a single-step prediction that might look fine. But in weather forecasting you're doing autoregressive rollouts, feeding the model's output back in again and again, so those small errors accumulate. Eventually you see blow-ups, spurious energy building up at high frequencies, and the forecast just becomes unphysical.

So by replacing the FFT with spherical harmonic transforms, we respect the geometry and the rotational symmetry of the sphere. The question then is how you actually assess whether that helps, and we looked at it a few ways.

The first is simply long rollouts. Instead of only checking skill at a few days, we ran the model autoregressively for very long horizons, on the order of a year of simulated time, and checked whether it stays stable and doesn't drift or explode. The flat FNO-based version would degrade and become unstable much earlier, whereas the spherical version stayed stable over those long horizons.

The second is physical plausibility, not just pointwise error. Metrics like RMSE and anomaly correlation are standard, but at long lead times every model's pointwise skill decays toward climatology, so they don't tell you whether the dynamics are still sensible. So we looked at the energy spectrum, how energy is distributed across spatial scales, and whether it stays consistent with the reanalysis data. An unstable model tends to pile up energy at small scales or smooth everything out. With the spherical formulation the spectra stayed much more realistic over the rollout.

The third is checking for artifacts directly: looking at behavior near the poles, at the seams of the grid, and whether there are any directional biases that come from treating the sphere as a rectangle.

And on top of that we still compare short- and medium-range skill against the operational physics-based models, because stability doesn't mean much if you give up accuracy. The nice thing is you get both: comparable skill in the medium range, plus a model that behaves physically over long horizons.

The broader lesson for me is that the right inductive bias matters. Building in the geometry and symmetries of the problem, and working in function space rather than on a fixed grid, is what gives you stability for free instead of needing ad hoc tricks to keep the rollouts from blowing up. That becomes really important when you want to go beyond weather into things like climate-scale simulation and large ensembles, where you're running these models for very long times.

fable-5.1.text:
That's actually one of my favorite results from the whole FourCastNet line of work, because it's such a clean illustration of why the right inductive bias matters more than more parameters.

So the first FourCastNet used an adaptive Fourier neural operator, which was great for throughput, but it treated the globe as a flat periodic rectangle. That's a lie, right? The lat-lon grid is just a projection. You have the poles collapsing to a single point, you have distortion, you have artificial seams. And when you roll a model out autoregressively, every one of those small inconsistencies gets fed back in as input. Six hours, twelve hours, you're fine. But by day five, day seven, you'd start to see artifacts near the poles, and then the whole thing would blow up, energy would accumulate in the wrong wavenumbers, and the fields would just stop looking like weather.

What we did with the spherical Fourier neural operator, this was Boris Bonev and Thorsten Kurth driving a lot of it, is replace the FFT with a spherical harmonic transform. So the global convolution respects the actual geometry of the sphere. Rotations are handled naturally, there's no privileged direction, the poles aren't special anymore.

And the stability improvement wasn't incremental. We went from rollouts that degrade on the order of a week to rollouts that stay physically plausible for a year. Over a thousand autoregressive steps. Now, I want to be careful, because at that horizon it's not a forecast anymore, nobody is predicting the weather a year out. But the point is the model stays on the attractor. The statistics remain climate-like. You can look at a year-long rollout and see realistic seasonal cycles, realistic jet streams, no blow-up. That's what you need if you want to use these models for ensembles, for climate-scale studies, for anything beyond medium-range weather.

The way I think about it is that the long rollout is a diagnostic for whether the model has learned the dynamics or just learned to fit the next frame. If you get the geometry wrong, it learns to patch over the geometry errors, and that patch is exactly what fails out of distribution. If you get the geometry right, the errors it makes are more like the atmosphere's own errors, and those don't compound in the same catastrophic way.

So I'd assess it as foundational. It's the difference between a nice demo and a tool you'd actually trust for science. And honestly, it's a lesson that generalizes well beyond weather. Whenever the data lives on a manifold, build the operator on the manifold. Don't make the network learn what you already know.

astra-6.text:
If you’re modeling global weather, the sphere is the natural geometry of the problem. When you flatten it onto a plane, you introduce distortions, especially near the poles, and those can become a source of error as you roll the model forward—feeding its predictions back in as inputs.

So I’d assess stability over those longer rollouts, not just look at one-step accuracy. Does the error grow more slowly? Does the model preserve realistic large-scale patterns, or does it start producing artifacts? You want a controlled comparison with the same data and comparable model capacity. Respecting the spherical geometry is a useful inductive bias, but it doesn’t by itself guarantee stability or that the model has learned the right physics.
